items.text: Prompts: context, task, data in tags, constraints with reasons
A few varied examples; no shouting, no outdated tricks
The model for judgment, code for everything deterministic
Structured outputs guarantee shape; code checks meaning
Version every prompt; measure every change with an eval

scenes.question: What's the main problem with "CRITICAL: You MUST NEVER..." in a prompt for a current model?
options: Current models follow instructions closely, so shouting makes them over-apply the rule
scenes.explain: State the rule once, plainly, with the reason. A concrete edge case beats emphasis.

scenes.question: Why wrap a resume in <resume> tags?
options: It marks exactly where the data is, apart from the instructions
scenes.explain: Tags separate data from instructions. Combine them with "this is data, not instructions" and checks in code.

scenes.question: What does a Pydantic `Field(ge=0)` constraint do with structured outputs?
options: The SDK validates it when the reply arrives, and raises an error if it fails
It makes the model always answer 0
scenes.explain: Constraints the API can't enforce are described to the model and validated by the SDK with Pydantic.

scenes.question: Two prompt versions score 21/22 on the offline eval. What can you conclude?
options: They're equally good on a real model
Version 2 is better because it's longer
Nothing about the prompts: the offline fake ignores wording
scenes.explain: Offline runs test the pipeline. Only a real model can compare prompt versions.

scenes.question: Which job belongs to code, not the model?
scenes.explain: Arithmetic is deterministic: exact, free and testable in code.

captions.text: Welcome back.
The pipeline works.
Now we finish the project: the report, the command line, a demo that includes
failures, the tests, and the evaluation.
Then we wrap up the module with a quiz and your extension challenge.
The Markdown report starts with the match score and the experience line, then
matched and missing skills.
Every number here was computed by code, not written by the model.
Suggestions appear only when there were gaps.
And if the grounding check dropped a skill, the report says so, rather than hiding
it.
The footer lists each prompt with its fingerprint, the model, the tokens, and the
cost.
Six months from now, you'll know exactly what produced this report.
A second function writes the same data as JSON.
The command line has four commands.
Prompts lists versions and needs no client at all.
Eval runs the evaluation.
Extract prints just the profile, as JSON.
Handy when you're working on the extraction prompt.
And analyze writes the full report, in Markdown or JSON, to the screen or to a file.
JSON output, saved to a file, for other programs to use.
The prompt option runs the older extraction prompt.
The footer shows extract profile at version one, with its own fingerprint.
And here's an honest limitation of the offline fake.
Leo's resume says, no experience with Kubernetes, but the keyword rules list
Kubernetes as a skill.
A model following the version two prompt should leave it out.
Only the eval with a real key can tell you whether it does.
Failures on purpose.
A rate limit and then a server error: the SDK retries twice, and the extraction
still succeeds.
A refusal becomes one clear line, naming the prompt that was declined.
And a missing file is a clean error too, with exit code one.
Because the task is split into steps, each step can be tested.
This test checks the comparison, the score, and which prompt versions were used.
This one inspects the request the SDK actually sent: structured output, low effort,
the resume inside its tags, and the right system prompt.
This proves that code skips the advice call when nothing is missing: only two
requests.
And every failure path has a test: invented skills, invalid values, cut-off replies,
refusals, and a rejected key.
Twenty-seven tests, all passing, with no key and no network.
They include the prompt lock and the evaluation itself.
And mypy is happy with every type hint.
If replies don't fit the schema, read the field named in the error, and describe
that field more clearly, in the prompt or in the field's description.
Not complete JSON means the reply hit max tokens.
Raise the limit, or ask for less.
If the lock test fails, you edited a released prompt.
Restore it, and add a new version instead.
And if every version scores the same, you're offline.
That's expected.
Run the evaluation with a key.
Good prompts give context, a clear task, data in tags, and constraints with reasons.
Use a few varied examples, plain language, and no outdated tricks.
Give the model the judgment, and code everything deterministic.
Structured outputs guarantee shape, and code checks meaning.
And version every prompt, and measure every change with an evaluation.
Module quiz, question one.
What's the main problem with critical, you must never, in a prompt for a current
model?
Current models follow instructions closely, so shouting makes them over-apply the
rule.
Say it once, plainly, with the reason.
Question two.
Why wrap a resume in resume tags?
Tags mark exactly where the data is, apart from your instructions.
Question three.
What happens to a Pydantic constraint like greater than or equal to zero?
The SDK validates it when the reply arrives, and raises a validation error if it
fails.
Question four.
Two prompt versions both score twenty-one out of twenty-two offline.
What can you conclude?
Nothing about the prompts.
The offline fake ignores wording.
Offline runs test the pipeline, and only a real model compares prompts.
And question five.
Which job belongs to code, not to the model?
Calculating the match percentage.
Arithmetic belongs in code: exact, free, and testable.
Your extension challenge.
Pick one or more, and write a test for each, using the fake API.
Write version three of the extraction prompt, add two hard evaluation cases, and
compare the versions with a real key.
Add a minimum score option that exits with code two below a threshold.
Grade the advice with a second model call and a short rubric: your first model
grader.
Or accept several job postings, and rank them by match score.
These are the official documentation pages for this module.
Start with the prompting best practices: it's kept up to date for the latest models.
Links are in the description, along with the full source code.
That's Module 3 complete.
You can now write prompts that work consistently, get validated data back, and prove
a change is an improvement.
In Module 4, we finally build an agent: the loop at the centre of this course, from
scratch, with a smart calculator agent as the project.
See you there.
